# MiniMax-Music3, bf16 — radiance container

[MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-Music3](https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-Music3) — songs with vocals from
lyrics and a description — as a single `.rad` container for the
[radiance](https://codeberg.org/StillDeadcode/radiance) inference engine (AMD RDNA4, ROCm).

| | |
|---|---|
| File | `minimax-music3-bf16.rad` — 20.48 GiB |
| Weights | bf16 throughout: the language model and the depth decoder as they ship; the DiT, the condition encoder and the vocoder cast from f32 (their norms, snake alphas, Fourier projection and layer mix stay f32) |
| Audio | 44.1 kHz stereo, 16-bit; up to six minutes |
| Needs | radiance 1.8.0 or newer (MiniMax-Music3 support comes with 1.8.0); one card or two |

## Serve

```sh
# two cards; one card works too (drop --tp 2)
radiance --model minimax-music3-bf16.rad --tp 2 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000

curl -s http://localhost:8000/v1/audio/speech -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "input": "[verse]\nMorning light filtering through the pine\n[chorus]\nSoftly the world begins to breathe",
  "instructions": "Genre: acoustic pop. BPM: 96. Warm and intimate. Vocals: soft female lead.",
  "duration": 30, "seed": 7}' -o song.wav
```

The server answers OpenAI's `POST /v1/audio/speech` as SGLang-Omni reads it for music:

- `input` is the lyrics, with the model's section tags such as `[verse]` and `[chorus]`;
  `instructions` describe the song (genre, tempo, key, mood, vocals, instruments). Both are required.
- `duration` (seconds) or `max_new_tokens` (frames, 25 a second) sets the length; without either the
  song runs until the model ends it, usually at the end of the lyrics.
- `seed` makes a song repeatable on the same deployment; `num_inference_steps` (30) and
  `guidance_scale` (1.7) are the denoiser's; `response_format` is `wav` or `pcm`.
- `"stream_format": "audio"` sends the song as it is made, eight seconds at a time;
  `"stream_format": "sse"` sends it as `speech.audio.delta` events.

On two Radeon AI PRO R9700s (gfx1201) a song is made at about the speed it plays: 10 s of audio in
10.8 s with the first audio at 8.5 s, 12 s in 12.7 s. On one card, 4 s in 7.3 s. Up to four songs
are made at once.

Against diffusers' pipeline from the same seed, the language model's hidden state is 1.55% from the
reference's (the reference's own bf16 against its f32: 1.27%), the DiT's velocity 1.3% (1.8%), and
100 frames of audio on one card are 29.0 dB SNR from it (28.7 dB).

## How this file was made

```sh
rad-convert MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-Music3 --recipe minimax-music3-bf16.recipe -o minimax-music3-bf16.rad
```

`MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-Music3` is the downloaded diffusers pipeline directory. The recipe
(`minimax-music3-bf16.recipe` in this repository) names what changes dtype; the vocoder's weight
norm is folded in f32 before its cast:

```
dit.*.ln1.*                          cast dtype=f32
dit.*.ln2.*                          cast dtype=f32
dit.t.fourier                        cast dtype=f32
dit.*                                cast dtype=bf16
cond.mix.*                           cast dtype=f32
cond.*                               cast dtype=bf16
voc.*.alpha                          cast dtype=f32
voc.*                                cast dtype=bf16
```

## License

MiniMax-Music3 is licensed under the MiniMax-Music3 Community License (`LICENSE` in this repository,
Copyright (c) 2026 MiniMax), which includes its Acceptable Use Policy. A commercial product or
service that uses it must display "MiniMax-Music3" on its user interface, and one whose yearly
revenue exceeds 20 million US dollars needs MiniMax's prior written authorization. This container is
a modified copy: the DiT, the condition encoder and the vocoder are cast from f32 to bf16 (the
vocoder's weight norm folded first), and everything is repacked into one `.rad` file.
MiniMax-Music3 was fine-tuned from Qwen3-8B (Apache License 2.0).

--- license: apache-2.0 language: - en - zh base_model: - openbmb/MiniCPM4-0.5B pipeline_tag: text-to-speech library_name: voxcpm tags: - text-to-speech - speech - speech generation - voice cloning --- ## 🎙️ VoxCPM: Tokenizer-Free TTS for Context-Aware Speech Generation and True-to-Life Voice Cloning [![Project Page](https://img.shields.io/badge/Project%20Page-GitHub-blue)](https://github.com/OpenBMB/VoxCPM/) [![MiniCPM Wiki](https://img.shields.io/badge/Docs-ReadTheDocs-8CA1AF)](https://modelbest.feishu.cn/wiki/UtWxwcERfiRIpIkBOjuc3h9tn1D) [![Technical Report](https://img.shields.io/badge/Technical%20Report-Arxiv-red)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.24650)[![Live Playground](https://img.shields.io/badge/Live%20PlayGround-Demo-orange)](https://huggingface.co/spaces/OpenBMB/VoxCPM-Demo) [![Samples](https://img.shields.io/badge/Audio%20Samples-Page-green)](https://openbmb.github.io/VoxCPM-demopage) - VoxCPM1.5 [![Hugging Face](https://img.shields.io/badge/%F0%9F%A4%97%20Hugging%20Face-OpenBMB-yellow)](https://huggingface.co/openbmb/VoxCPM1.5) [![ModelScope](https://img.shields.io/badge/ModelScope-OpenBMB-purple)](https://modelscope.cn/models/OpenBMB/VoxCPM1.5)
## 🎉 VoxCPM1.5 Updates **Release Date:** December 5, 2025 VoxCPM1.5 brings improvements in audio quality and efficiency: | Feature | VoxCPM | VoxCPM1.5 | |---------|------------|------------| | **Audio VAE Sampling Rate** | 16kHz | 44.1kHz | | **LM Token Rate** | 12.5Hz | 6.25Hz | | **Patch Size** | 2 | 4 | | **SFT Support** | ✅ | ✅ | | **LoRA Support** | ✅ | ✅ | **Key Improvements:** - 🔊 **Higher Quality**: 44.1kHz sampling rate preserves more high-frequency details for better voice cloning - ⚡ **More Efficient**: Reduced token rate (6.25Hz) lowers computational cost while maintaining performance - 🎓 **Fine-tuning Support**: Train personalized voice models with SFT or LoRA **Note**: Output quality depends on the prompt speech quality. VoxCPM-0.5B remains fully supported with backward compatibility. ## 📚 Model Overview VoxCPM is a novel tokenizer-free Text-to-Speech (TTS) system that redefines realism in speech synthesis. By modeling speech in a continuous space, it overcomes the limitations of discrete tokenization and enables two flagship capabilities: context-aware speech generation and true-to-life zero-shot voice cloning. Unlike mainstream approaches that convert speech to discrete tokens, VoxCPM uses an end-to-end diffusion autoregressive architecture that directly generates continuous speech representations from text. Built on [MiniCPM-4](https://huggingface.co/openbmb/MiniCPM4-0.5B) backbone, it achieves implicit semantic-acoustic decoupling through hierachical language modeling and FSQ constraints, greatly enhancing both expressiveness and generation stability.
### 🚀 Key Features - **Context-Aware, Expressive Speech Generation** - VoxCPM comprehends text to infer and generate appropriate prosody, delivering speech with remarkable expressiveness and natural flow. It spontaneously adapts speaking style based on content, producing highly fitting vocal expression trained on a massive 1.8 million-hour bilingual corpus. - **True-to-Life Voice Cloning** - With only a short reference audio clip, VoxCPM performs accurate zero-shot voice cloning, capturing not only the speaker’s timbre but also fine-grained characteristics such as accent, emotional tone, rhythm, and pacing to create a faithful and natural replica. - **High-Efficiency Synthesis** - VoxCPM supports streaming synthesis with a Real-Time Factor (RTF) as low as 0.17 on a consumer-grade NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU, making it possible for real-time applications. ## Quick Start ### 🔧 Install from PyPI ``` sh pip install voxcpm ``` ### 1. Model Download (Optional) By default, when you first run the script, the model will be downloaded automatically, but you can also download the model in advance. - Download VoxCPM1.5 ``` from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download snapshot_download("openbmb/VoxCPM1.5") ``` - Or Download VoxCPM-0.5B ``` from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download snapshot_download("openbmb/VoxCPM-0.5B") ``` - Download ZipEnhancer and SenseVoice-Small. We use ZipEnhancer to enhance speech prompts and SenseVoice-Small for speech prompt ASR in the web demo. ``` from modelscope import snapshot_download snapshot_download('iic/speech_zipenhancer_ans_multiloss_16k_base') snapshot_download('iic/SenseVoiceSmall') ``` ### 2. Basic Usage ```python import soundfile as sf import numpy as np from voxcpm import VoxCPM model = VoxCPM.from_pretrained("openbmb/VoxCPM1.5") # Non-streaming wav = model.generate( text="VoxCPM is an innovative end-to-end TTS model from ModelBest, designed to generate highly expressive speech.", prompt_wav_path=None, # optional: path to a prompt speech for voice cloning prompt_text=None, # optional: reference text cfg_value=2.0, # LM guidance on LocDiT, higher for better adherence to the prompt, but maybe worse inference_timesteps=10, # LocDiT inference timesteps, higher for better result, lower for fast speed normalize=False, # enable external TN tool, but will disable native raw text support denoise=False, # enable external Denoise tool, but it may cause some distortion and restrict the sampling rate to 16kHz retry_badcase=True, # enable retrying mode for some bad cases (unstoppable) retry_badcase_max_times=3, # maximum retrying times retry_badcase_ratio_threshold=6.0, # maximum length restriction for bad case detection (simple but effective), it could be adjusted for slow pace speech ) sf.write("output.wav", wav, model.tts_model.sample_rate) print("saved: output.wav") # Streaming chunks = [] for chunk in model.generate_streaming( text = "Streaming text to speech is easy with VoxCPM!", # supports same args as above ): chunks.append(chunk) wav = np.concatenate(chunks) sf.write("output_streaming.wav", wav, model.tts_model.sample_rate) print("saved: output_streaming.wav") ``` ### 3. CLI Usage After installation, the entry point is `voxcpm` (or use `python -m voxcpm.cli`). ```bash # 1) Direct synthesis (single text) voxcpm --text "VoxCPM is an innovative end-to-end TTS model from ModelBest, designed to generate highly expressive speech." --output out.wav # 2) Voice cloning (reference audio + transcript) voxcpm --text "VoxCPM is an innovative end-to-end TTS model from ModelBest, designed to generate highly expressive speech." \ --prompt-audio path/to/voice.wav \ --prompt-text "reference transcript" \ --output out.wav \ # --denoise # (Optinal) Voice cloning (reference audio + transcript file) voxcpm --text "VoxCPM is an innovative end-to-end TTS model from ModelBest, designed to generate highly expressive speech." \ --prompt-audio path/to/voice.wav \ --prompt-file "/path/to/text-file" \ --output out.wav \ # --denoise # 3) Batch processing (one text per line) voxcpm --input examples/input.txt --output-dir outs # (optional) Batch + cloning voxcpm --input examples/input.txt --output-dir outs \ --prompt-audio path/to/voice.wav \ --prompt-text "reference transcript" \ # --denoise # 4) Inference parameters (quality/speed) voxcpm --text "..." --output out.wav \ --cfg-value 2.0 --inference-timesteps 10 --normalize # 5) Model loading # Prefer local path voxcpm --text "..." --output out.wav --model-path /path/to/VoxCPM_model_dir # Or from Hugging Face (auto download/cache) voxcpm --text "..." --output out.wav \ --hf-model-id openbmb/VoxCPM1.5 --cache-dir ~/.cache/huggingface --local-files-only # 6) Denoiser control voxcpm --text "..." --output out.wav \ --no-denoiser --zipenhancer-path iic/speech_zipenhancer_ans_multiloss_16k_base # 7) Help voxcpm --help python -m voxcpm.cli --help ``` ### 4. Start web demo You can start the UI interface by running `python app.py`, which allows you to perform Voice Cloning and Voice Creation. ### 5. Fine-tuning VoxCPM1.5 supports both full fine-tuning (SFT) and LoRA fine-tuning, allowing you to train personalized voice models on your own data. See the [Fine-tuning Guide](https://github.com/OpenBMB/VoxCPM/blob/main/docs/finetune.md) for detailed instructions. **Quick Start:** ```bash # Full fine-tuning python scripts/train_voxcpm_finetune.py \ --config_path conf/voxcpm_v1.5/voxcpm_finetune_all.yaml # LoRA fine-tuning python scripts/train_voxcpm_finetune.py \ --config_path conf/voxcpm_v1.5/voxcpm_finetune_lora.yaml ``` ## 👩‍🍳 A Voice Chef's Guide Welcome to the VoxCPM kitchen! Follow this recipe to cook up perfect generated speech. Let’s begin. --- ### 🥚 Step 1: Prepare Your Base Ingredients (Content) First, choose how you’d like to input your text:. 1. Regular Text (Classic Mode) - ✅ Keep "Text Normalization" ON. Type naturally (e.g., "Hello, world! 123"). The system will automatically process numbers, abbreviations, and punctuation using WeTextProcessing library. 2. Phoneme Input (Native Mode) - ❌ Turn "Text Normalization" OFF. Enter phoneme text like {HH AH0 L OW1} (EN) or {ni3}{hao3} (ZH) for precise pronunciation control. In this mode, VoxCPM also supports native understanding of other complex non-normalized text—try it out! - **Phoneme Conversion**: For Chinese, phonemes are converted using pinyin. For English, phonemes are converted using CMUDict. Please refer to the relevant documentation for more details. --- ### 🍳 Step 2: Choose Your Flavor Profile (Voice Style) This is the secret sauce that gives your audio its unique sound. #### 1. Cooking with a Prompt Speech (Following a Famous Recipe) - A prompt speech provides the desired acoustic characteristics for VoxCPM. The speaker's timbre, speaking style, and even the background sounds and ambiance will be replicated. - **For a Clean, Denoising Voice:** - ✅ Enable "Prompt Speech Enhancement". This acts like a noise filter, removing background hiss and rumble to give you a pure, clean voice clone. However, this will limit the audio sampling rate to 16kHz, restricting the cloning quality ceiling. - **For High-Quality Audio Cloning (Up to 44.1kHz):** - ❌ Disable "Prompt Speech Enhancement" to preserve all original audio information, including background atmosphere, and support audio cloning up to 44.1kHz sampling rate. #### 2. Cooking au Naturel (Letting the Model Improvise) - If no reference is provided, VoxCPM becomes a creative chef! It will infer a fitting speaking style based on the text itself, thanks to the text-smartness of its foundation model, MiniCPM-4. - **Pro Tip**: Challenge VoxCPM with any text—poetry, song lyrics, dramatic monologues—it may deliver some interesting results! --- ### 🧂 Step 3: The Final Seasoning (Fine-Tuning Your Results) You're ready to serve! But for master chefs who want to tweak the flavor, here are two key spices. #### CFG Value (How Closely to Follow the Recipe) - **Default**: A great starting point. - **Voice sounds strained or weird?** Lower this value. It tells the model to be more relaxed and improvisational, great for expressive prompts. - **Need maximum clarity and adherence to the text?** Raise it slightly to keep the model on a tighter leash. - **Short sentences?** Consider increasing the CFG value for better clarity and adherence. - **Long texts?** Consider lowering the CFG value to improve stability and naturalness over extended passages. #### Inference Timesteps (Simmering Time: Quality vs. Speed) - **Need a quick snack?** Use a lower number. Perfect for fast drafts and experiments. - **Cooking a gourmet meal?** Use a higher number. This lets the model "simmer" longer, refining the audio for superior detail and naturalness. --- Happy creating! 🎉 Start with the default settings and tweak from there to suit your project. The kitchen is yours! --- ## ⚠️ Risks and limitations - General Model Behavior: While VoxCPM has been trained on a large-scale dataset, it may still produce outputs that are unexpected, biased, or contain artifacts. - Potential for Misuse of Voice Cloning: VoxCPM's powerful zero-shot voice cloning capability can generate highly realistic synthetic speech. This technology could be misused for creating convincing deepfakes for purposes of impersonation, fraud, or spreading disinformation. Users of this model must not use it to create content that infringes upon the rights of individuals. It is strictly forbidden to use VoxCPM for any illegal or unethical purposes. We strongly recommend that any publicly shared content generated with this model be clearly marked as AI-generated. - Current Technical Limitations: Although generally stable, the model may occasionally exhibit instability, especially with very long or expressive inputs. Furthermore, the current version offers limited direct control over specific speech attributes like emotion or speaking style. - Bilingual Model: VoxCPM is trained primarily on Chinese and English data. Performance on other languages is not guaranteed and may result in unpredictable or low-quality audio. - This model is released for research and development purposes only. We do not recommend its use in production or commercial applications without rigorous testing and safety evaluations. Please use VoxCPM responsibly. ## 📄 License The VoxCPM model weights and code are open-sourced under the Apache-2.0 license.

## Latest Release: Chatterbox Multilingual V3 **Chatterbox Multilingual V3** is the latest general-purpose multilingual TTS model in the Chatterbox family. It keeps the same 0.5B model size while improving speaker similarity, reducing hallucinations, and producing more natural, conversational speech across languages. V3 is designed for broad language coverage like V2, but with stronger stability and more expressive generation. It is the recommended multilingual model for users who want one voice cloning model that works across many languages. Try it in the [Chatterbox Multilingual TTS V3 Space](https://huggingface.co/spaces/ResembleAI/Chatterbox-Multilingual-TTS-V3). Alongside V3, we are releasing the **Single Language Pack**: dedicated finetunes for priority languages where tighter quality control, stronger language-specific behavior, and more specialized speech generation are valuable. - **Broad Multilingual Coverage:** Designed as the main general-purpose multilingual Chatterbox model, supporting wide language coverage similar to V2. - **Single Language Pack:** Dedicated single-language models provide stronger specialization and quality control where language- and regional-dialect-specific performance matters most. - **More Consistent Speaker Similarity:** Improves voice identity and accent preservation across languages, making cross-language voice cloning more stable and reliable. - **Reduced Hallucination:** V3 is optimized to reduce unwanted continuation, repetition, and off-prompt speech, especially in cases where earlier multilingual models were less stable. ## Model Zoo Choose the right Chatterbox model for your application. | Model | Size | Languages | Key Features | Best For | Demo | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | **Chatterbox Multilingual V3** | **500M** | **23+** | Improved speaker similarity, reduced hallucinations, more natural multilingual speech | Global applications, localization, cross-language voice cloning | [Demo](https://huggingface.co/spaces/ResembleAI/Chatterbox-Multilingual-TTS-V3) | | **Single Language Pack** | 500M each | 6 dedicated finetunes | Language- and region-specific quality control | Priority languages and dialect-sensitive applications | [Demos](#single-language-pack) | | Chatterbox | 500M | English | CFG and exaggeration tuning | General zero-shot TTS with creative controls | [Demo](https://huggingface.co/spaces/ResembleAI/Chatterbox) | **09/04 🔥 Introducing Chatterbox Multilingual in 23 Languages!** We're excited to introduce **Chatterbox** and **Chatterbox Multilingual**, [Resemble AI's](https://resemble.ai) production-grade open source TTS models. Chatterbox Multilingual supports **Arabic, Danish, German, Greek, English, Spanish, Finnish, French, Hebrew, Hindi, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Malay, Dutch, Norwegian, Polish, Portuguese, Russian, Swedish, Swahili, Turkish, Chinese** out of the box. Licensed under MIT, Chatterbox has been benchmarked against leading closed-source systems like ElevenLabs, and is consistently preferred in side-by-side evaluations. Whether you're working on memes, videos, games, or AI agents, Chatterbox brings your content to life. It's also the first open source TTS model to support **emotion exaggeration control**, a powerful feature that makes your voices stand out. Try it now on our [Hugging Face Gradio app.](https://huggingface.co/spaces/ResembleAI/Chatterbox) If you like the model but need to scale or tune it for higher accuracy, check out our competitively priced TTS service (link). It delivers reliable performance with ultra-low latency of sub 200ms—ideal for production use in agents, applications, or interactive media. # Key Details - Chatterbox Multilingual V3, a 0.5B general-purpose multilingual TTS model supporting 23 languages - Dedicated single-language finetunes for Chinese, LatAm Spanish, Brazilian Portuguese, Spain Spanish, Portugal Portuguese, and Hindi - SoTA zeroshot English TTS - 0.5B Llama backbone - Unique exaggeration/intensity control - Ultra-stable with alignment-informed inference - Trained on 0.5M hours of cleaned data - Watermarked outputs - Easy voice conversion script - [Outperforms ElevenLabs](https://podonos.com/resembleai/chatterbox) # Tips - **General Use (TTS and Voice Agents):** - The default settings (`exaggeration=0.5`, `cfg=0.5`) work well for most prompts. - If the reference speaker has a fast speaking style, lowering `cfg` to around `0.3` can improve pacing. - **Expressive or Dramatic Speech:** - Try lower `cfg` values (e.g. `~0.3`) and increase `exaggeration` to around `0.7` or higher. - Higher `exaggeration` tends to speed up speech; reducing `cfg` helps compensate with slower, more deliberate pacing. ***Note:*** Ensure that the reference clip matches the specified language tag. Otherwise, language transfer outputs may inherit the accent of the reference clip’s language. ***To mitigate this, set the CFG weight to 0.*** # Installation ``` pip install chatterbox-tts ``` # Usage ```python import torchaudio as ta from chatterbox.tts import ChatterboxTTS model = ChatterboxTTS.from_pretrained(device="cuda") text = "Ezreal and Jinx teamed up with Ahri, Yasuo, and Teemo to take down the enemy's Nexus in an epic late-game pentakill." wav = model.generate(text) ta.save("test-1.wav", wav, model.sr) # If you want to synthesize with a different voice, specify the audio prompt AUDIO_PROMPT_PATH="YOUR_FILE.wav" wav = model.generate(text, audio_prompt_path=AUDIO_PROMPT_PATH) ta.save("test-2.wav", wav, model.sr) ``` # Multilingual Quickstart ```python import torchaudio as ta from chatterbox.mtl_tts import ChatterboxMultilingualTTS multilingual_model = ChatterboxMultilingualTTS.from_pretrained( device="cuda", t3_model="v3", ) # To use the legacy V2 multilingual checkpoint, omit t3_model or pass t3_model="v2". french_text = "Bonjour, comment ça va? Ceci est le modèle de synthèse vocale multilingue Chatterbox, il prend en charge 23 langues." wav_french = multilingual_model.generate(french_text, language_id="fr") ta.save("test-french.wav", wav_french, multilingual_model.sr) chinese_text = "你好，今天天气真不错，希望你有一个愉快的周末。" wav_chinese = multilingual_model.generate(chinese_text, language_id="zh") ta.save("test-chinese.wav", wav_chinese, multilingual_model.sr) ``` See `example_tts.py` for more examples. ## Single Language Pack The Single Language Pack provides dedicated finetunes for priority languages and regional variants. [Cosyvoice](https://github.com/FunAudioLLM/CosyVoice) - [HiFT-GAN](https://github.com/yl4579/HiFTNet) - [Llama 3](https://github.com/meta-llama/llama3) # Built-in PerTh Watermarking for Responsible AI Every audio file generated by Chatterbox includes [Resemble AI's Perth (Perceptual Threshold) Watermarker](https://github.com/resemble-ai/perth) - # MOSS-TTS-Nano-100M Core ML

Compiled streaming Core ML graphs for MOSS-TTS-Nano-100M and the companion
MOSS-Audio-Tokenizer-Nano. Generates 48 kHz stereo audio, with optional reference
audio conditioning. The host owns SentencePiece tokenization and sampling.

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Speech model parameters | 117,311,232 |
| Codec inference parameters (weight normalization folded) | 21,042,560 |
| Format | Compiled Core ML ML Programs (`.mlmodelc`) |
| Precision | Global/codec decoder: FP16 weights/matrix operations, FP32 normalization/rotary phases/residuals; local decoder/encoder: FP32; state: FP16 |
| Graph size | 367.6 MB total |
| Context | 1024 prompt + generated rows |
| Prefill | Up to 256 rows per call; longer prompts use consecutive calls |
| Audio | 48,000 Hz, two channels, 3,840 samples/channel per frame (12.5 frames/s) |
| Codec tokens | 16 codebooks, 1,024 entries each |
| Deployment | macOS 15+ / iOS 18+; local measurements use macOS only |

## Files

| File | Size | Description |
|---|---:|---|
| `GlobalDecoder.mlmodelc` | 220.8 MB | mixed_float16_float32 GlobalDecoder |
| `LocalDecoder.mlmodelc` | 78.7 MB | float32 LocalDecoder |
| `CodecDecoder.mlmodelc` | 22.6 MB | mixed_float16_float32 CodecDecoder |
| `CodecEncoder.mlmodelc` | 45.5 MB | float32 CodecEncoder |
| `tokenizer.model` | 0.47 MB | SentencePiece BPE vocabulary |
| `tokenizer_swift.json` | 1.01 MB | Original vocabulary, scores and compiled normalization map for native Swift |
| `config.json` | Small | Graph contracts, source revisions and measured parity/latency |
| `run_coreml.py` | Small | Python synthesis/reference-encoding example |
| `benchmark_coreml.py` | Small | Fresh-process memory and first-token/audio benchmark |
| `requirements-runtime.txt` | Small | Pinned runtime-only dependencies |
| `LICENSE` | Small | Apache License 2.0 |

The global and codec decoders keep normalization, rotary phases and residual
operations in full precision to preserve rotary position accuracy in longer audio.
The local decoder keeps all calculations in full precision to avoid drift across
local steps. The encoder also uses full precision to protect residual code selection.

## Measured checks

These are sequential synthetic graph checks against unmodified upstream PyTorch,
including multiple cache updates and two complete local frames. Per-call medians
include graph work and Python prediction overhead. They are not an utterance
throughput benchmark. Codec calls produce or consume one 80 ms frame.

Machine: `macOS-26.6.2-arm64-arm-64bit`.

| Graph | Compute units | Parity (higher is better) | Median prediction |
|---|---|---|---:|
| GlobalDecoder | CPU_ONLY | 0.9997798 minimum cosine | 8.55 ms |
| GlobalDecoder | CPU_AND_GPU | 0.9999997 minimum cosine | 28.67 ms |
| LocalDecoder | CPU_ONLY | 0.9999838 minimum cosine | 0.58 ms |
| LocalDecoder | CPU_AND_GPU | 0.9999839 minimum cosine | 1.02 ms |
| CodecDecoder | CPU_ONLY | 0.9998652 minimum cosine | 3.34 ms |
| CodecDecoder | CPU_AND_GPU | 0.9999966 minimum cosine | 9.35 ms |
| CodecEncoder | CPU_ONLY | 100.0% token agreement | 3.72 ms |
| CodecEncoder | CPU_AND_GPU | 100.0% token agreement | 10.94 ms |

## Speech smoke checks

38 tests passed, including reference voice cloning, long prompts, rotary positions up to 16,000 and a 10.4-second codec comparison beyond every attention window.

Sample timings below exclude model loading. Time/audio duration below 1 means faster than real time. CPU was faster for this short utterance on the Apple M5 Pro, so the example defaults to `CPU_ONLY`; `--compute-unit CPU_AND_GPU` selects GPU execution.

| File | Compute units | Audio duration | Time/audio duration | First audio | Whisper tiny.en transcript |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| `samples/hello-gpu.wav` | CPU_AND_GPU | 2.72 s | 0.376 | 162 ms | Hello from Koi Mill. |
| `samples/hello.wav` | CPU_ONLY | 1.76 s | 0.294 | 79 ms | Hello from CoreML. |
| `samples/voice-clone.wav` | CPU_AND_GPU | 3.12 s | 0.413 | 80 ms | The weather is nice today. |

These are short smoke checks. The GPU greeting's acronym differs in automatic transcription; the CPU greeting and reference-conditioned sentence match their inputs after case/punctuation/spacing normalization. Full results are in `speech_validation.json`.


## Process memory and token latency

Measured on Apple M5 Pro in a fresh runtime-only Python process per backend. First/warm means the first request and the median of five subsequent requests. Every request has fresh model state. OS/Core ML disk caches were not cleared.

| Backend | Peak RSS (MiB) | First audio token, first/warm (ms) | First audio, first/warm (ms) | Warm time/audio duration | Model load (s) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| CPU_ONLY | 658.0 | 62 / 44 | 82 / 57 | 0.289 | 0.98 |
| CPU_AND_GPU | 635.5 | 87 / 21 | 178 / 47 | 0.422 | 1.18 |

Latency includes tokenization, state creation and prefill, and excludes model loading. The first token is the first sampled codec token. First audio is the first decoded 80 ms stereo frame, after all 16 codebooks. RSS includes the complete Python/Core ML worker, with neither PyTorch nor ASR loaded. Lower latency, time/audio duration and RSS are better. CPU generates the full utterance faster; the warmed GPU returns the first token sooner. Full measurements and definitions are in `performance.json`.


## Voice-cloning memory and latency

Same isolated runtime-only Python method, using the saved 2.72-second stereo reference `samples/hello-gpu.wav`, text `The weather is nice today.`, seed 1. First and warm requests include reading, resampling/padding, loading the codec encoder and encoding the reference. Cached requests reuse reference codes. Warm/cached are medians of five requests each, with fresh generation state. Initial loading of the three synthesis graphs is excluded from latency.

| Backend | Peak RSS (MiB) | First token, first/warm (ms) | Cached first token (ms) | First audio, first/warm/cached (ms) | Warm/cached time/audio duration |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| CPU_ONLY | 779.2 | 542 / 203 | 52 | 563 / 216 / 65 | 0.324 / 0.270 |
| CPU_AND_GPU | 731.1 | 649 / 225 | 24 | 741 / 245 / 48 | 0.471 / 0.400 |

These measurements exercise the complete reference-conditioning path. They do not measure speaker similarity. CPU and GPU can sample different output durations; compare time/audio duration for throughput. Results describe Python on this Mac, not the native Swift runtime or iPhone. Full data: `cloning_performance.json`.


## Usage

Install `coremltools==9.0`, `numpy==1.26.4`, `sentencepiece==0.2.1`,
`soundfile==0.13.1`, and `scipy==1.15.3`. Synthesis needs neither PyTorch nor
Transformers. Run on macOS with the four compiled directories beside the script:

```bash
python run_coreml.py "Hello from Core ML." --output hello.wav
python run_coreml.py "A new sentence." --reference reference.wav --output cloned.wav
```

```python
from pathlib import Path
import soundfile as sf
from run_coreml import Pipeline

pipeline = Pipeline(Path("."), compute_unit="CPU_ONLY")
audio, codes, report = pipeline.synthesize("Hello from Core ML.")
sf.write("hello.wav", audio, 48000)
print(report)
```

Reference inputs may be mono or stereo; the example resamples them to 48 kHz and
pads the final 80 ms frame. Clone mode uses reference audio without a transcript,
matching the released model's prompt format. Use authorized reference recordings.
Sampled generation uses a fixed seed of 0, text temperature 1.0, audio temperature
0.8, audio top-k 25, audio top-p 0.95 and repetition penalty 1.2. Use `--seed` to
change the sampled voice/take. `--greedy` is available for diagnostics; greedy
generation can repeat without reaching end-of-speech in the original model too.
Generation raises an error if the context or frame limit would truncate speech.

## Graph contracts

- `GlobalDecoder`: `input_ids [1,T,17] int32`, `position [1] int32` ->
  `hidden [1,768] float32`. New state per utterance. The first call has position 0;
  later calls append rows at the next contiguous position.
- `LocalDecoder`: `global_hidden [1,768] float32`, `previous_token [1] int32`,
  `step [1] int32` -> `text_logits [1,2]`, `audio_logits [1,1024]`.
  Step 0 clears the local cache and predicts continue/end (IDs 9/7).
  Steps 1 through 16 predict the audio codebooks in order.
- `CodecEncoder`: `audio [1,2,3840] float32`, `frame [1] int32` ->
  `codes [1,1,16] int32`. New state per reference; frame starts at 0.
- `CodecDecoder`: `codes [1,1,16] int32`, `frame [1] int32` ->
  `audio [1,2,3840] float32`. New state per generated utterance; frame starts at 0.

State shapes and their exported names are in `config.json`. Keep every state with
its utterance/reference. The codec retains the upstream sliding attention windows.

# BgTTS-38M V2 — Bulgarian Text-to-Speech with Voice Cloning

A lightweight **38M parameter** encoder-decoder TTS model for **Bulgarian and English** speech synthesis with **zero-shot voice cloning** via [MioCodec](https://huggingface.co/Aratako/MioCodec-25Hz-24kHz).

**V2 improvements over V1:**
- **Speaker normalization** — stable voice quality across all reference audio files
- **Larger training dataset** — 1,537 hours (vs 1,172h in V1)
- **BF16 training** — more stable gradients, no GradScaler needed
- **Zero dropout** — better utilization of model capacity
- **20 epochs** with careful LR scheduling

## Audio Samples

### Female Voice (Bulgarian)

<audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/beleata74/BgTTS-38M-V2/resolve/main/samples/sample_female_bg1.wav"></audio>

### Female Voice (English)

### Male Voice 1 (Bulgarian)

### Male Voice 1 (English)

### Male Voice 2 (Bulgarian)

<audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/beleata74/BgTTS-38M-V2/resolve/main/samples/sample_male2_bg1.wav"></audio>

### Male Voice 2 (English)

<audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/beleata74/BgTTS-38M-V2/resolve/main/samples/sample_male2_en1.wav"></audio>

## Key Features

- **Bilingual**: Native Bulgarian + English in a single model
- **Voice cloning**: Zero-shot — just provide 3-10 seconds of reference audio
- **Tiny footprint**: 146 MB inference checkpoint, runs on CPU
- **Fast**: RTF ~0.3 on both GPU and CPU (3.3× faster than real-time)
- **Speaker-stable**: V2's normalized speaker embedding ensures consistent quality regardless of reference audio

## 🎙️ Voice Cloning

This model supports zero-shot voice cloning — it can generate speech in any voice given just a short reference audio clip. No fine-tuning needed.

### How it Works

1. Provide a reference audio (3-10 seconds of clear speech, WAV format, ideally 24kHz)
2. MioCodec extracts a 128-dimensional speaker embedding (`global_embedding`)
3. The embedding is **L2-normalized** and scaled by a learned parameter (`spk_scale`) before being added to the decoder
4. The same embedding is used for MioCodec waveform reconstruction

### V2 Improvement: Speaker Normalization

In V1, the speaker embedding had 7× larger norm than content tokens, causing the model to over-rely on the reference audio for pronunciation quality. V2 normalizes the speaker vector to unit norm, ensuring:
- **Consistent quality** across all reference voices
- The model learns speech patterns from data, not from speaker shortcuts
- Reference audio only affects **timbre**, not articulation

## Model Architecture

| Component | Details |
|---|---|
| Text Encoder | 4-layer bidirectional Transformer (d=384, 6 heads, ff=1536) |
| Audio Decoder | 8-layer causal Transformer (d=384, 6 heads, ff=1536) with cross-attention |
| Speaker Injection | L2-normalized Linear(128 → 384) with learned scale, additive bias |
| Audio Codec | [MioCodec](https://huggingface.co/Aratako/MioCodec-25Hz-24kHz) 25Hz, 1 codebook, 12800 codes, 24kHz output |
| Total Parameters | 38.2M (Encoder: 9.6M, Decoder: 28.6M) |
| Activations | SwiGLU |
| Normalization | RMSNorm (pre-norm) |
| Positional Encoding | Learned (encoder), RoPE (decoder) |
| Embeddings | Tied decoder (lm_head = token_embedding) |
| KV-Cache | Yes (for fast autoregressive inference) |

### Tokenizer

Character-level tokenizer supporting 146 characters:
- Bulgarian Cyrillic (А-Я, а-я)
- English Latin (A-Z, a-z)
- Digits, punctuation, whitespace

Total vocabulary: **12,955 tokens** (9 special + 146 text + 12,800 audio codes)

## Training

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Data** | 728K samples, **1,537 hours** total |
| Bulgarian | ~620K samples (~1,368 hours) |
| English | ~108K samples (~169 hours) |
| **Epochs** | 20 |
| **LR Schedule** | Cosine decay, peak 7e-5, warmup 2 epochs, min 5e-6 |
| **Batch Size** | 64 |
| **Optimizer** | AdamW (betas=0.9, 0.999), weight decay 0.01 |
| **Precision** | BF16 (no GradScaler) |
| **Dropout** | 0.0 (unnecessary — model is 38M, data is 1,537h) |
| **Final Loss** | 5.04 |
| **Hardware** | NVIDIA RTX 5090 (32GB VRAM) |

### Why Zero Dropout?

With only 38M parameters and 138M audio tokens (1,537 hours), the model has **0.28 parameters per token**. Overfitting is mathematically impossible — the model is severely underfitting the data. Dropout only slows convergence without providing any regularization benefit.

## Quick Start

### Requirements

```bash
pip install torch torchaudio soundfile miocodec
```

### Python API

```python
import torch
from model import load_for_inference
from tokenizer import TTSTokenizer
from codec import CodecV6
from inference import generate

device = "cuda"  # or "cpu"

# Load model
model = load_for_inference("checkpoint_inference.pt", device=device)
tokenizer = TTSTokenizer()
codec = CodecV6(device=device)

# Get speaker embedding from reference audio
ref = codec.encode("reference_speaker.wav")
speaker_emb = ref["global_embedding"].to(device)

# Generate
codes = generate(
    model, tokenizer,
    text="Здравейте, как сте днес?",
    speaker_emb=speaker_emb,
    temperature=0.3,
    top_k=250,
    max_new_tokens=512,
    device=device,
)

# Decode to audio
if codes is not None:
    wav = codec.tokens_to_wav(codes, speaker_emb, "output.wav")
```

### CLI

```bash
python inference.py \
  --checkpoint checkpoint_inference.pt \
  --text "Здравейте, как сте днес?" \
  --speaker-wav reference.wav \
  --output output.wav \
  --temperature 0.3
```

### Web UI (Gradio)

```bash
python server.py
# Opens at http://localhost:7860
```

### Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `--temperature` | 0.3 | Sampling temperature (lower = stable, higher = expressive) |
| `--top-k` | 250 | Top-k filtering |
| `--top-p` | 0.95 | Nucleus sampling threshold |
| `--rep-penalty` | 1.1 | Repetition penalty on recent tokens |
| `--max-tokens` | 512 | Maximum decoder steps (~20 seconds) |

**Recommended temperature: 0.3** for clean, stable output. Use 0.5-0.7 for more expressive/varied speech.

## ⚠️ Important: Sentence Length

> The encoder supports up to **256 characters** (~18 seconds of audio). For longer texts, `inference.py` automatically splits by sentence boundaries and concatenates the audio. No manual splitting needed.

```
model.py                  # Architecture (TTSEncoderDecoder + speaker normalization)
tokenizer.py              # Character-level tokenizer
codec.py                  # MioCodec wrapper
inference.py              # Inference pipeline with KV-cache + sentence splitting
train.py                  # Training script (BF16)
server.py                 # Gradio web UI
samples/                  # Audio samples (3 voices × 2 languages × 3 texts)
```

## Performance

### Benchmarks

| Hardware | RTF | Speed | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Intel i3-9100F (CPU)** | **0.30** | **3.3× real-time** | **Windows 10, CPU-only, no GPU** |

### CPU-only Deployment (Tested on Windows 10)

| Component | Disk Space |
|---|---|
| Python venv (PyTorch CPU + deps) | 654 MB |
| BgTTS-38M-V2 (checkpoint + code) | 146 MB |
| MioCodec (auto-downloaded, cached) | 499 MB |
| WavLM base+ (auto-downloaded, cached) | 872 MB |
| **Total** | **2.12 GB** |

No NVIDIA GPU, no CUDA, no special drivers needed. Works on any x86-64 machine with Python 3.8+.

## Comparison with Other Models

| Model | Parameters | Size | Languages | Voice Cloning | Open Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **BgTTS-38M V2** | **38M** | **146 MB** | BG + EN | ✅ | ✅ |
| Kokoro-82M | 82M | ~200 MB | Multi | ❌ | ✅ |
| XTTS-v2 | ~467M | ~1.8 GB | 16 | ✅ | ✅ |
| CSM-1B | 1B | ~4 GB | EN | ✅ | ✅ |
| Dia-1.6B | 1.6B | ~6.4 GB | EN | ✅ | ✅ |

BgTTS-38M V2 is the **smallest TTS model with voice cloning** we are aware of, and the **only** open-source TTS model with native Bulgarian language support.

## Limitations

- Best with sentences up to ~18 seconds. Longer texts are auto-split by `inference.py`.
- Bulgarian quality is superior to English (82% of training data is Bulgarian).
- Voice cloning quality depends on reference audio clarity — use clean recordings without background noise.
- No explicit prosody control (pitch, speed) — these are implicitly learned from data.
- Character-level tokenizer may struggle with rare Unicode characters outside the supported set.

Highlights - 🌍 **30-Language Multilingual** — No language tag needed; input text in any supported language directly - 🎨 **Voice Design** — Generate a novel voice from a natural-language description alone (gender, age, tone, emotion, pace…); no reference audio required - 🎛️ **Controllable Cloning** — Clone any voice from a short clip, with optional style guidance to steer emotion, pace, and expression while preserving timbre - 🎙️ **Ultimate Cloning** — Provide reference audio + its transcript for audio-continuation cloning; every vocal nuance faithfully reproduced - 🔊 **48kHz Studio-Quality Output** — Accepts 16kHz reference; outputs 48kHz via AudioVAE V2's built-in super-resolution, no external upsampler needed - 🧠 **Context-Aware Synthesis** — Automatically infers appropriate prosody and expressiveness from text content - ⚡ **Real-Time Streaming** — RTF as low as ~0.3 on NVIDIA RTX 4090, and ~0.13 accelerated by [Nano-VLLM](https://github.com/a710128/nanovllm-voxcpm) - 📜 **Fully Open-Source & Commercial-Ready** — Apache-2.0 license, free for commercial use Supported Languages (30) Arabic, Burmese, Chinese, Danish, Dutch, English, Finnish, French, German, Greek, Hebrew, Hindi, Indonesian, Italian, Japanese, Khmer, Korean, Lao, Malay, Norwegian, Polish, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, Swahili, Swedish, Tagalog, Thai, Turkish, Vietnamese Chinese Dialects: 四川话, 粤语, 吴语, 东北话, 河南话, 陕西话, 山东话, 天津话, 闽南话 ## Quick Start ### Installation ```bash pip install voxcpm ``` **Requirements:** Python ≥ 3.10, PyTorch ≥ 2.5.0, CUDA ≥ 12.0 · [Full Quick Start →](https://voxcpm.readthedocs.io/en/latest/quickstart.html) ### Text-to-Speech ```python from voxcpm import VoxCPM import soundfile as sf model = VoxCPM.from_pretrained("openbmb/VoxCPM2", load_denoiser=False) wav = model.generate( text="VoxCPM2 brings multilingual support, creative voice design, and controllable voice cloning.", cfg_value=2.0, inference_timesteps=10, ) sf.write("output.wav", wav, model.tts_model.sample_rate) ``` ### Voice Design Put the voice description in parentheses at the start of `text`, followed by the content to synthesize: ```python wav = model.generate( text="(A young woman, gentle and sweet voice)Hello, welcome to VoxCPM2!", cfg_value=2.0, inference_timesteps=10, ) sf.write("voice_design.wav", wav, model.tts_model.sample_rate) ``` ### Controllable Voice Cloning ```python # Basic cloning wav = model.generate( text="This is a cloned voice generated by VoxCPM2.", reference_wav_path="speaker.wav", ) sf.write("clone.wav", wav, model.tts_model.sample_rate) # Cloning with style control wav = model.generate( text="(slightly faster, cheerful tone)This is a cloned voice with style control.", reference_wav_path="speaker.wav", cfg_value=2.0, inference_timesteps=10, ) sf.write("controllable_clone.wav", wav, model.tts_model.sample_rate) ``` ### Ultimate Cloning Provide both the reference audio and its exact transcript for maximum fidelity. Pass the same clip to both `reference_wav_path` and `prompt_wav_path` for highest similarity: ```python wav = model.generate( text="This is an ultimate cloning demonstration using VoxCPM2.", prompt_wav_path="speaker_reference.wav", prompt_text="The transcript of the reference audio.", reference_wav_path="speaker_reference.wav", ) sf.write("hifi_clone.wav", wav, model.tts_model.sample_rate) ``` ### Streaming ```python import numpy as np chunks = [] for chunk in model.generate_streaming(text="Streaming is easy with VoxCPM!"): chunks.append(chunk) wav = np.concatenate(chunks) sf.write("streaming.wav", wav, model.tts_model.sample_rate) ``` ## Model Details | Property | Value | |---|---| | Architecture | Tokenizer-free Diffusion Autoregressive (LocEnc → TSLM → RALM → LocDiT) | | Backbone | Based on MiniCPM-4, totally 2B parameters | | Audio VAE | AudioVAE V2 (asymmetric encode/decode, 16kHz in → 48kHz out) | | Training Data | 2M+ hours multilingual speech | | LM Token Rate | 6.25 Hz | | Max Sequence Length | 8192 tokens | | dtype | bfloat16 | | VRAM | ~8 GB | | RTF (RTX 4090) | ~0.30 (standard) / ~0.13 (Nano-vLLM) | ## Performance VoxCPM2 achieves state-of-the-art or competitive results on major zero-shot and controllable TTS benchmarks. See the [GitHub repo](https://github.com/OpenBMB/VoxCPM#-performance) for full benchmark tables (Seed-TTS-eval, CV3-eval, InstructTTSEval, MiniMax Multilingual Test). ## Fine-tuning VoxCPM2 supports both full SFT and LoRA fine-tuning with as little as 5–10 minutes of audio: ```bash # LoRA fine-tuning (recommended) python scripts/train_voxcpm_finetune.py \ --config_path conf/voxcpm_v2/voxcpm_finetune_lora.yaml # Full fine-tuning python scripts/train_voxcpm_finetune.py \ --config_path conf/voxcpm_v2/voxcpm_finetune_all.yaml ``` See the [Fine-tuning Guide](https://voxcpm.readthedocs.io/en/latest/finetuning/finetune.html) for full instructions. ## Limitations - Voice Design and Style Control results may vary between runs; generating 1–3 times is recommended to obtain the desired output. - Performance varies across languages depending on training data availability. - Occasional instability may occur with very long or highly expressive inputs. - **Strictly forbidden** to use for impersonation, fraud, or disinformation. AI-generated content should be clearly labeled. ## Citation ```bibtex @article{voxcpm2_2026, title = {VoxCPM2: Tokenizer-Free TTS for Multilingual Speech Generation, Creative Voice Design, and True-to-Life Cloning}, author = {VoxCPM Team}, journal = {GitHub}, year = {2026}, } @article{voxcpm2025, title = {VoxCPM: Tokenizer-Free TTS for Context-Aware Speech Generation and True-to-Life Voice Cloning}, author = {Zhou, Yixuan and Zeng, Guoyang and Liu, Xin and Li, Xiang and Yu, Renjie and Wang, Ziyang and Ye, Runchuan and Sun, Weiyue and Gui, Jiancheng and Li, Kehan and Wu, Zhiyong and Liu, Zhiyuan}, journal = {arXiv preprint arXiv:2509.24650}, year = {2025}, } ``` ## License Released under the [Apache-2.0](https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0) license, free for commercial use. It produces natural Egyptian speech with seamless **Arabic ↔ English code-switching**, ships **19 built-in voices**, supports **zero-shot voice cloning**, and includes a robust Egyptian-Arabic **text normalization** pipeline plus **true streaming** for long text.
> **Why "VoiceTut"?** *Tut* — after the boy-king **Tutankhamun** (توت عنخ آمون) — anchors the model in Egyptian identity, just as our companion ASR model **[QwenCleo-ASR](https://github.com/MohammedAly22/qwencleo-asr)** is named after **Cleopatra**. Together they form an Egyptian speech stack: **Cleo listens, Tut speaks.** 🎙️🗣️ ## 🆕 What's new in v2 **VoiceTut-TTS-v2** is a more capable model that **supports Arabic diacritics (التشكيل)**. Plain text works exactly as before, and if a word is pronounced wrong you can fix it by adding diacritics to that word — the model follows them. ```python tts.synthesize("انا مْخَطَّط للموضوع ده", speaker="Mohammed", output="fixed.wav") ``` The previous weights remain available on the [`v1` branch](https://huggingface.co/mohammedaly22/VoiceTut-TTS/tree/v1). ## 🔗 Links - 🎧 **Audio demo (VoiceTut vs. base OmniVoice):** https://mohammedaly22.github.io/VoiceTuT-TTS/ - 🚀 **Interactive Space:** https://huggingface.co/spaces/mohammedaly22/VoiceTut-TTS - 💻 **GitHub (code, notebooks):** https://github.com/MohammedAly22/VoiceTuT-TTS - 📦 **PyPI:** https://pypi.org/project/voicetut-tts/ ## ✨ Features - 🎯 **Egyptian-first** — fine-tuned specifically on Egyptian Arabic, not generic MSA. - 🔀 **Code-switching** — handles real Arabic + English mixed speech (`عندي meeting بكرة`). - 🗣️ **19 built-in voices** — male & female speakers. - 🧬 **Zero-shot cloning** — clone any voice from a few seconds of reference audio. - ✍️ **Diacritics support (v2)** — add التشكيل to any word to control its pronunciation. - 🔢 **Robust normalization** — numbers, dates, times, currencies, phones, emails, URLs, abbreviations + an English→Arabic name map. - ⚡ **True streaming** — long text is split into sentences and yielded as audio chunks. ## 📦 Installation ```bash # PyTorch matching your CUDA (see https://pytorch.org) pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu121 # OmniVoice backbone (not on PyPI — install from GitHub) pip install git+https://github.com/k2-fsa/OmniVoice.git pip install voicetut-tts ``` ## 🚀 Usage ```python from voicetut_tts import VoiceTutTTS tts = VoiceTutTTS.from_pretrained("mohammedaly22/VoiceTut-TTS") # 1) Built-in speaker tts.synthesize("ازيك عامل ايه النهاردة؟", speaker="Mohammed", output="out.wav") # 2) Zero-shot voice cloning tts.synthesize("النهارده الجو حلو اوي", ref_audio="my_voice.wav", ref_text="ده الصوت بتاعي", output="clone.wav") # 3) Code-switching + generation params tts.synthesize("عندي meeting الساعة 3:30 ومعايا ال presentation", speaker="Yasmin", num_step=48, guidance_scale=2.5, speed=1.05, output="cs.wav") # 4) Fix a word's pronunciation with diacritics tts.synthesize("دي عِشْرة عمر يا صاحبي", speaker="Ahmed", output="fixed.wav") ``` Streaming long text: ```python for sr, chunk in tts.stream(long_paragraph, speaker="Ahmed"): play(chunk) # plays each sentence as it's generated tts.synthesize_long(long_paragraph, "long.wav", speaker="Ahmed") ``` ## 🗣️ Built-in Voices | | Male | Female | |---|---|---| | Names | Ahmed, Ali, Hassan, Karim, Mahmoud, Mohammed, Mostafa, Ramy, Shaker, Tareq, Yehia, Youssef | Hadeer, Hanan, Mariam, Rana, Sarah, Yasmin, Yara | Each voice ships with a reference clip. Browse and listen in the [Space](https://huggingface.co/spaces/mohammedaly22/VoiceTut-TTS). ## 📊 Performance > Measured on a single **NVIDIA T4 (Colab)**, `float16`, `num_step=32`. Reproduce with [`examples/04_evaluation.ipynb`](https://github.com/MohammedAly22/VoiceTuT-TTS/blob/main/examples/04_evaluation.ipynb). | Metric | Value | |---|---| | Real-time factor (RTF, mean) | **1.13×** | | RTF (best) | **0.49×** | | Time-to-first-audio (streaming) | **1.68 s** | | Peak VRAM (fp16) | **2.93 GB** | | WER — Egyptian Arabic | **0.40** | | WER — English | **0.07** | | Speaker similarity (cloning, cosine) | **0.83** | | Naturalness (UTMOS, 1–5) | **3.47** | | Sampling rate | 24 kHz | > On A100 / H100 expect markedly lower RTF and TTFA. ## 🏗️ Model - **Base model:** [k2-fsa/OmniVoice](https://github.com/k2-fsa/OmniVoice) (Qwen3-0.6B text backbone + Higgs audio tokenizer) - **Language id:** `arz` (Egyptian Arabic), with English code-switching (`en`) ## ⚠️ Responsible Use Voice cloning is provided to enable **beneficial** use cases — voice assistants, accessibility, educational and creative content. **Do not** use it to impersonate real people, produce deceptive or misleading audio, or harm, harass, or defraud anyone. # Drama 3 MLX 4-bit

**Built with Fish Audio.**

[Fish Audio Drama 3](https://huggingface.co/fishaudio/drama-3) converted for [mlx-audio](https://github.com/Blaizzy/mlx-audio) on Apple Silicon. This is an unofficial community conversion; Fish Audio did not release or endorse it.

- routed experts: 4-bit, dequantized from the block-FP8 release
- dense projections and audio tower: 8-bit
- 22 GB on disk, about 26 GB peak memory while generating

## Usage

Drama 3 support was merged into mlx-audio in [#1018](https://github.com/Blaizzy/mlx-audio/pull/1018), after the 0.5.9 release. Until the next release, install from `main`:

```bash
pip install "mlx-audio @ git+https://github.com/Blaizzy/mlx-audio"
```

```python
from mlx_audio.tts.utils import load_model

model = load_model("mlx-community/fish-audio-drama-3-4bit")

for result in model.generate(
    text="[sighs] Fine. If we miss it, it's on you.",
    ref_audio="reference.wav",
    ref_text="Transcript of the reference clip.",
    stream=True,
    first_chunk_frames=4,
):
    print(result.audio.shape)  # 44.1 kHz chunks
```

```bash
python -m mlx_audio.tts.generate --model mlx-community/fish-audio-drama-3-4bit \
    --text "[sighs] Fine. If we miss it, it's on you." \
    --ref_audio reference.wav --ref_text "Transcript of the reference clip." \
    --temperature 0.7 --top_p 0.7 --top_k 30
```

Speaker tags (`<|speaker:0|>` to `<|speaker:15|>`), multiple references and streaming are described in the [model docs](https://github.com/Blaizzy/mlx-audio/blob/main/docs/models/tts/fish-drama3.md).

## Quality and speed

On an M3 Max:

- 22 ms per frame (46 ms of audio), about 2x real time
- first streamed audio in 160 to 200 ms once a voice is cached
- teacher-forced against the PyTorch reference: backbone hidden cosine 0.995, semantic top-1 86%

## Conversion

Made with mlx-audio's converter:

```bash
python -m mlx_audio.tts.models.fish_drama3.convert --src drama-3 --dst drama-3-mlx-4bit \
    --expert-bits 4 --dense-bits 8 --tower-bits 8
```

The unquantized weights are at [mlx-community/fish-audio-drama-3-bf16](https://huggingface.co/mlx-community/fish-audio-drama-3-bf16).

`NOTICE` lists every change to the original weights.

# SoulX-Podcast-1.7B for MLX (8-bit)

[SoulX-Podcast-1.7B](https://huggingface.co/Soul-AILab/SoulX-Podcast-1.7B) by Soul AI Lab, converted for Apple silicon. It speaks a multi-speaker dialogue (up to 4 speakers, Mandarin and English) turn by turn, each turn hearing the ones before it, in voices cloned from a short reference clip and its transcript per speaker.

This conversion is made for [AudioSmith](https://github.com/hehehai/AudioSmith)'s engine (Swift + MLX), which runs it in its stories' 「整场对话」 (whole dialogue) mode. It is not a drop-in replacement for the official PyTorch checkpoint.

## Files

| File | What |
|---|---|
| `config.json`, `model.safetensors` | The Qwen3-1.7B language model (vocabulary 159,488: text, 6,561 speech tokens, tags), quantized to 8 bits with mlx-lm (group size 64, bfloat16 scales; 8.5 bits per weight). The output layer is tied to the embeddings. |
| `s3gen.safetensors` | CosyVoice2's flow matching (encoder + CFM decoder), HiFT vocoder (`mel2wav.*`) and CAM++ speaker encoder (`speaker_encoder.*`), float32, keyed for mlx-audio-swift's `CausalMaskedDiffWithXvec`. |
| tokenizer files, `generation_config.json`, `soulxpodcast_config.json` | Upstream's, unchanged. |
| `conversion.json` | The converter and its commit. |
| `LICENSE`, `NOTICE` | Apache-2.0 and the attributions. |

The S3 speech tokenizer (25 Hz) is not included: use [mlx-community/S3TokenizerV2](https://huggingface.co/mlx-community/S3TokenizerV2).

## How it was converted

With [`scripts/soulx/convert.py`](https://github.com/hehehai/AudioSmith/blob/main/scripts/soulx/convert.py) from Soul-AILab/SoulX-Podcast-1.7B at revision `7d381e3aa4f2ac9e23201b57957fd0499f8f2fd1`:

- the language model: `mlx_lm` convert, 8 bits, group size 64, bfloat16;
- `flow.pt` and `hift.pt`: modules renamed, weight norm folded, convolutions transposed to MLX's layout;
- `campplus.onnx`: initializers renamed; the batch norms the ONNX exporter had folded into convolutions are written back as identity batch norms carrying the folded biases.

The flow, HiFT and CAM++ weights are byte-identical upstream to [FunAudioLLM/CosyVoice2-0.5B](https://huggingface.co/FunAudioLLM/CosyVoice2-0.5B)'s.

## Parity with the official code

AudioSmith's engine was checked against the official PyTorch implementation (soulxpodcast @ 5ac9c0e, transformers 4.57.1) on the same inputs:

| Stage | Result |
|---|---|
| 16 kHz log-mel / S3 tokens | max difference 1.3·10⁻⁴; 100 % of tokens equal |
| CAM++ x-vector | cosine 0.999998 |
| 24 kHz flow mel | max difference 1.5·10⁻⁴ |
| Prompt token ids | identical |
| Language model logits, float32 | identical top 100, KL < 10⁻⁴ |
| This 8-bit model vs float32 | argmax equal, top-100 overlap 99, KL 0.0014 |
| Sampling (repetition penalty → temperature → top-k → top-p, RAS) | processed scores identical |
| Flow matching with fixed noise | correlation 1.00000 |
| HiFT waveform (no random phase/noise) | SNR 52 dB |

Sampling must follow upstream: repetition penalty 1.25 on the current turn's tokens, temperature 0.6, top-k 100, top-p 0.9, repetition-aware sampling (window 25, ratio 0.2), 8 to 3,000 tokens a turn, stop at token 151675. (Dropping temperature and top-k/p, as one community port did, raises the character error rate from about 1 % to 4–10 %.)

## Licence

Apache License 2.0, as the original model; see `LICENSE` and `NOTICE`.

## Usage disclaimer

From the original model card: this model is for research and legitimate use. **Do not clone anyone's voice without their consent, do not impersonate people, and do not use it for fraud, deception or any illegal purpose.** You are responsible for what you generate with it.

## Credits

- [SoulX-Podcast](https://github.com/Soul-AILab/SoulX-Podcast) (Soul AI Lab, Northwestern Polytechnical University and others; arXiv 2510.23541).
- [CosyVoice2](https://github.com/FunAudioLLM/CosyVoice) (Alibaba Tongyi SpeechTeam): flow matching, HiFT, S3 tokenizer.

# Fish Audio Drama 3, MLX 6-bit

Built with Fish Audio.

A community MLX conversion of [Fish Audio Drama 3](https://huggingface.co/fishaudio/drama-3), made directly from the original checkpoint. This is not an official or endorsed Fish Audio release.

- Routed experts use **6-bit affine quantization**, group size 64.
- Dense projections and the audio tower use **8-bit affine quantization**, group size 64.
- Other small tensors retain the types chosen by MLX Audio's converter. The Fish S1 DAC codec is unchanged and unquantized.
- About **31.8 GB** of checkpoint files. Short reference-conditioned GPU tests peaked at about **34.2 GB** of MLX memory on an M5 Max. Allow room for macOS and other apps; a 48 GB or larger Mac is a practical starting point. That memory estimate is not a guarantee for long or multi-reference prompts.

No model was trained or fine-tuned. No personal voice recordings or synthetic training data were used to produce these weights. This was not re-quantized from the 4-bit model.

## Use with MLX Audio

Drama 3 requires an MLX Audio version with the merged Drama 3 implementation. The tested upstream source was commit `d35a8038131f0de33b7ae6da3f2d5b69523b1c3e`, reporting MLX Audio 0.5.9, with MLX 0.32.3. The PyPI 0.5.9 wheel predates Drama 3 support.

```sh
pip install "mlx-audio[tts] @ git+https://github.com/Blaizzy/mlx-audio@d35a8038131f0de33b7ae6da3f2d5b69523b1c3e"
```

```python
from mlx_audio.tts.utils import load_model

model = load_model("maxxrubin/fish-audio-drama-3-6bit")
for result in model.generate(
    text="[whispers] Keep this between us. [laughs] I think we made it work.",
    ref_audio="reference.wav",
    ref_text="The exact words spoken in your reference recording.",
    temperature=1.0,
    top_p=0.9,
    top_k=30,
    max_tokens=500,
    stream=True,
    first_chunk_frames=4,
):
    print(result.audio.shape, result.sample_rate)
```

Use a clear reference with an accurate transcript. Audio output is mono at 44.1 kHz. Speaker tags `<|speaker:0|>` through `<|speaker:15|>`, inline expressions, streaming, and long-text chunking use the normal [MLX Audio Drama 3 API](https://github.com/Blaizzy/mlx-audio/blob/d35a8038131f0de33b7ae6da3f2d5b69523b1c3e/docs/models/tts/fish-drama3.md).

For a reproducible synthetic reference, download `examples/reference.wav`. Its transcript is:

> Hello there. This six bit version of Drama Three is running locally on Apple Silicon.

That clip was generated by this checkpoint without a human reference. The other example WAVs use it as their reference.

## Checks performed

These are GPU smoke checks, not a voice quality benchmark. Apple M5 Max with 128 GB unified memory, seed 42, temperature 1.0, top-p 0.9, top-k 30, 500 maximum frames per section, and the synthetic reference above:

| Prompt | Audio duration | Generation time | Audio frames |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Plain | 5.20 s | 3.04 s | 112 |
| Expressive | 3.90 s | 1.73 s | 84 |
| Dialogue | 2.55 s | 1.23 s | 55 |

All three runs returned finite, non-silent PCM audio, finished before the frame limit, and had zero clipped samples. Read `smoke-tests.json` for exact inputs and measurements. Timing uses a warm disk cache and includes streaming. It is not a controlled performance comparison.

Without a reference, sampling can produce quiet output or continue until the frame cap. This happened in preliminary tests on this checkpoint and, for the same expressive prompt, on the existing MLX Community 4-bit model. Reference conditioning resolved those cases in the three checks above. This does not establish a general failure rate. Try a reference, another seed, or another sampling recipe when a take stalls. No ASR, speaker-similarity, or listening study was performed, so no quality advantage over 4-bit or 8-bit is claimed.

## Conversion

Original source: `fishaudio/drama-3` at revision `b2b5ee998034b2975720906c815e7fb0e9f007bd`. Original routed experts are block-FP8. The official MLX Audio converter dequantized them to BF16 before applying 6-bit quantization. All 120 routed-expert projection entries were checked for 6-bit weights and group size 64.

```python
from pathlib import Path
from shutil import copyfile
from mlx_audio.tts.models.fish_drama3.convert import convert

convert(
    Path("drama-3-original"),
    Path("drama-3-mlx-6bit"),
    expert_bits=6,
    dense_bits=8,
    tower_bits=8,
    expert_group_size=64,
    codec=False,
)
# Reuse the unchanged codec from the pinned MLX Community conversion.
copyfile("drama-3-mlx-4bit/codec.safetensors", "drama-3-mlx-6bit/codec.safetensors")
```

The codec came from `mlx-community/fish-audio-drama-3-4bit`, revision `cc639e27aba7edb73429d3e3806f471dcd79d316`. Its SHA-256 is recorded in `conversion.json`. Source weights and the codec were verified against their published SHA-256 hashes before conversion. See `conversion.json` for package versions and `NOTICE` for the changes made to the original materials.

# MOSS-TTSD v1.0 for MLX (8-bit)

[MOSS-TTSD v1.0](https://huggingface.co/OpenMOSS-Team/MOSS-TTSD-v1.0) by OpenMOSS (MOSI.AI), with its [MOSS-Audio-Tokenizer](https://huggingface.co/OpenMOSS-Team/MOSS-Audio-Tokenizer), converted for Apple silicon. It speaks a whole multi-speaker dialogue (1 to 5 speakers; trained on 20 languages, Mandarin and English first) as one recording, in voices cloned from a short reference clip and its transcript per speaker.

This conversion is made for [AudioSmith](https://github.com/hehehai/AudioSmith)'s engine (Swift + MLX), which runs it in its stories' 「整场对话」 (whole dialogue) mode. It is not a drop-in replacement for the official PyTorch checkpoint, and needs a Mac with 24 GB of memory or more (about 12 GB while it speaks).

## Files

| File | What |
|---|---|
| `config.json`, `model-0000N-of-00002.safetensors`, `model.safetensors.index.json` | MOSS-TTSD (MossTTSDelay: a Qwen3-8B backbone, 16 audio-codebook embeddings, 17 heads), upstream's tensor names. Every Linear and Embedding is quantized to 8 bits (MLX affine, group size 64, bfloat16 scales and biases); norms stay bfloat16. 8.9 GB. |
| `codec.safetensors`, `codec_config.json` | MOSS-Audio-Tokenizer (24 kHz ↔ 12.5 frames a second): weight norm folded, 1×1 convolutions as matrices, attention projections renamed, the first 16 of 32 quantizers (the ones MOSS-TTSD reads); Linear layers whose input is a multiple of 64 in 8 bits (float32 scales), the rest float32. 2.0 GB. |
| tokenizer files, `generation_config.json`, `chat_template.jinja` | Upstream's, unchanged. |
| `conversion.json` | The converter and its commit. |
| `LICENSE`, `NOTICE` | Apache-2.0 and the attributions. |

## How it was converted

With [`scripts/mossttsd/convert.py`](https://github.com/hehehai/AudioSmith/blob/main/scripts/mossttsd/convert.py) from OpenMOSS-Team/MOSS-TTSD-v1.0 at revision `c7cd852d87aff71cab5bd2b9b05509cedc0ef1ba` and OpenMOSS-Team/MOSS-Audio-Tokenizer at `3cd226ba2947efa357ef453bcad111b6eafba782` (MLX 0.32).

## How AudioSmith runs it

As the official TTSD Space's voice-clone-and-continuation mode (OpenMOSS/MOSS-TTS `clis/moss_ttsd_app.py`): each speaker's clip is encoded alone into the user message's `Reference(s)`, all clips back to back are encoded once more as the start of the assistant's audio, and the text is every reference transcript as `[Sn] …` followed by the dialogue, through the Space's `normalize_text`. Sampling as the model card recommends and the official `generate()` does it: audio temperature 1.1, top-p 0.9, top-k 50, repetition penalty 1.1 (on every code already in the sequence, prompt included); text channel temperature 1.1, top-p 0.9, top-k 50. Decoding streams 8-second chunks, as the official processor does.

## Parity with the official code

AudioSmith's engine was checked against the official PyTorch implementation (transformers 5.0.0, torch 2.9.1, float32 on the CPU) on the same inputs:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Text normalization and the prompt (570 rows of text + 16 codebooks) | identical |
| Sampling: the processed distributions | identical |
| The delay-pattern generation loop (a tiny random model, greedy, 80 steps) | identical row for row |
| Language model logits, this file's weights in both (float32) | audio heads KL 6·10⁻¹¹, top-1 100 %; text head KL 2·10⁻¹² |
| Language model logits, this 8-bit model vs upstream bfloat16 weights | audio heads KL 0.013, top-1 76 % |
| Codec codes, this file's weights in both | 100 % equal; decoded waveform SNR 101–108 dB |
| Codec, this 8-bit codec vs upstream float32 | codebook 0 99 % equal, all 16 codebooks 86–90 %; decoded waveform SNR 34 dB |

On a MacBook Air M4 (24 GB), an 8-line Mandarin dialogue of two cloned speakers (about 28 s) takes about 36 s (0.79× real time, 11 rows a second) with a 12.2 GB MLX peak; character error rate 0–0.8 %, speaker similarity to the references 0.80–0.90.

# Pocket TTS, Q8_0

[Kyutai's Pocket TTS](https://huggingface.co/kyutai/pocket-tts) converted for Inklight, an iPhone app that reads books aloud on the device. The FlowLM transformer reads all its weights once for every frame it generates, which makes it memory-bound on a phone; with its linear layers in Q8_0 it reads a quarter as much and renders about 30 % faster, and the file is little more than half the size of the original.

## Files

`english_2026-04/model.q8.gguf`, about 129 MB: the `english_2026-04` model from [kyutai/pocket-tts-without-voice-cloning](https://huggingface.co/kyutai/pocket-tts-without-voice-cloning) with the FlowLM transformer's linear weights in Q8_0 and every other tensor in F16. The Mimi encoder, which turns audio into latents and is only used to clone a voice, is left out; in the release without voice cloning its weights are not usable anyway. Tensor names are those of the original `model.safetensors`.

The file needs the tokenizer and voice embeddings from Kyutai's repository, which are unchanged and not copied here, and the slower voice states in [inklight-app/paced-voices](https://huggingface.co/inklight-app/paced-voices) load into it the same way.

## How it was made

With `quantize_model` in [goocy/pocket-tts-ios](https://github.com/goocy/pocket-tts-ios) (branch `aloud`), a fork of the Rust port [UnaMentis/pocket-tts-ios](https://github.com/UnaMentis/pocket-tts-ios), which also loads the file. It is the same conversion the app used to run on each phone after downloading the original. Against the full-precision model, the transformer's hidden state differs by about 2 % (4.5 % in the worst frame of a 25-second utterance), and in listening tests the differences between renders followed the random seed, not the precision.

## Credits and licence

This is an adaptation of [Pocket TTS](https://huggingface.co/kyutai/pocket-tts) by Kyutai, licensed under the [Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) licence, and is released under the same licence. Kyutai's terms of use apply to it as to the original: it must not be used for voice impersonation or cloning without consent, to deceive, or to produce unlawful or harmful content.

Changes made: the transformer's linear weights were quantized to 8 bits, the other weights converted to 16-bit floats, and the voice-cloning encoder removed. Kyutai does not endorse this file or the app. It is provided without warranty.

# Pocket TTS Basque — 24-layer model (euskarazko ahots-sintesia)

A Basque (euskara) text-to-speech model based on [Pocket TTS](https://github.com/kyutai-labs/pocket-tts)
by Kyutai. This is the **24-layer "teacher" model** (~340 M parameters), obtained by fine-tuning Kyutai's
24-layer English model for Basque with the official new-language recipe, on the
[BSSD](https://huggingface.co/datasets/itzune/bssd) speech dataset. It supports zero-shot voice cloning
from a short reference clip.

A lighter 6-layer model distilled from this one, meant for real-time CPU use, will be released separately.

## Usage

With [`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) installed, no setup is needed:

```bash
uvx pocket-tts generate \
  --config hf://itzune/pocket-tts-basque-24l/basque_24l.yaml \
  --voice my_voice.wav \
  --text "Kaixo! Hau euskarazko ahots sintetiko bat da." \
  --output kaixo.wav
```

Python:

```python
from pocket_tts import TTSModel
import soundfile as sf

model = TTSModel.load_model(config="hf://itzune/pocket-tts-basque-24l/basque_24l.yaml")
voice = model.get_state_for_audio_prompt("my_voice.wav")      # 5-10 s of clean Basque speech
audio = model.generate_audio(voice, "Kaixo! Hau euskarazko ahots sintetiko bat da.")
sf.write("kaixo.wav", audio.squeeze().numpy(), model.sample_rate)  # 24 kHz
```

Notes:

- Write the text as it should be read: numbers, dates, abbreviations and symbols must be spelled out
  in words (e.g. `hogeita lau` rather than `24`). The dataset's normaliser
  ([`bssd.text_norm`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/itzune/bssd)) does this for standard Basque.
- The reference clip defines the voice. Only clone voices you have the right to use.
- `--config` also accepts a local copy of `basque_24l.yaml`; the weights and tokenizer are fetched from
  this repository.

## Evaluation

Held-out BSSD test sentences, 40 sentences per voice, scored with two independent Basque ASR systems
(`xezpeleta/whisper-large-v3-eu` and `HiTZ/stt_eu_conformer_transducer_large_v2`), UTMOS naturalness and
WavLM speaker similarity to the reference clip.

| voices | WER (Whisper) | WER (Conformer) | failure rate | WER excl. failures | UTMOS | speaker sim. |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 named prompts (dataset default voices) | 0.095 | 0.091 | 5.3 % | 0.042 | 3.59 | 0.958 |
| 5 unseen voices | 0.073 | 0.069 | 3.5 % | 0.033 | 3.61 | 0.961 |

The median sentence is read with no errors. "Failures" are sentences with WER > 0.5: in nearly all of
them the model continues the reference clip's own speech instead of reading the input text, a known
failure mode of prompt-conditioned models. It occurs more often with some reference clips than others
(from 0 % to about 20 % per voice in our tests); if a voice misbehaves, try a different or shorter clip.

## Training

- Base: Kyutai's 24-layer English Pocket TTS model (text embedding re-initialised for the new tokenizer).
- Tokenizer: SentencePiece, 4000 tokens, trained on the BSSD transcripts.
- Data: BSSD train split (about 350 k utterances, 450 h of synthetic Basque speech, 2,400+ voices,
  word-level alignments from `deepdml/wav2vec2-large-xls-r-300m-basque`).
- Recipe: official `finetune_language` configuration (learning rate 2e-4, effective batch 64,
  classifier-free-guidance dropout as upstream); the released weights are the EMA weights at step 40 k,
  chosen among the 40 k-80 k checkpoints by the evaluation above (later checkpoints had higher failure
  rates on unseen voices).

Training code, configs and evaluation scripts: https://github.com/xezpeleta/pocket-tts-eu

## Limitations

- Basque only; code-switched Spanish/French/English words are read with Basque phonetics.
- Prompt-continuation failures as described above; always check generated audio.
- Trained on synthetic speech: the voices in the dataset are themselves synthetic or re-synthesised,
  so the model may inherit artefacts of the dataset's teacher system. See the BSSD dataset card for the
  provenance of the voices and texts.

Model weights: CC-BY-4.0 (as the upstream Pocket TTS weights). Please cite Kyutai's Pocket TTS and the
BSSD dataset. Dataset: [itzune/bssd](https://huggingface.co/datasets/itzune/bssd) (CC-BY-SA-4.0).
